title: Umbra Systems — Dedicated capacity discovery: surge patterns & VPC evaluation
next_steps: Send Dedicated pricing and reserved node SKUs
Share SOC2 + network diagram and KMS notes
Schedule 60-min technical deep dive with infra team (Jonas + Samir)
Run a 48-72h burst simulation on a toy dataset (Jonas to propose script)
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-09-10 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonas (Redwood SE), Lena (Umbra - VP Eng), Samir (Umbra - Platform), Priya (Umbra - Security)

Summary: Quick qualification on Dedicated capacity, isolation requirements, burst model, and VPC/on-prem options. Customer is evaluating Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private; primary concerns are tail latency during marketing bursts, tenant isolation for PII, and encryption/KMS pathways.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Can we do quick intros? I'm Maya, AE on Redwood. Jonas is our performance SE.
[00:10] Lena: Hi, Lena here. We're trying to figure out how much reserved capacity to buy for our inference workloads for the new chat product. We have unpredictable marketing-driven spikes.
[00:20] Samir: Samir, platform eng. We run mostly GKE on GCP today, have internal endpoints for smaller models but need better cost predictability and latency.
[00:28] Priya: Priya - head of security. I'll focus on compliance, key management, and audit logs.
[00:33] Jonas: Quick log: we recommend starting with baseline profile then sizing warm pool for burst. But let's hear your pattern.

[02:15] Lena: Typical day-to-day 150 qps, median response ~120ms. But on campaigns we see up to 2k qps sustained for 10-30 minutes, and occasional spikes to 6k qps for <2 minutes. These bursts are the problematic ones — tail latency and cold-start errors.
[02:40] Maya: Helpful. Are those spikes mainly text-generation chat requests or embeddings?
[02:44] Samir: Mostly chat text-gen, some heavy context length (2-6k tokens) for session stitching.
[03:00] Jonas: Okay that matters for KV cache memory and sequence length. With Dedicated we can pin model variants and keep KV hot, reduces tail. For prewarm, we do a warm-pool of reserved nodes and optional hot pool prewarmed for peak windows.
[03:25] Lena: How deterministic is the warm pool? We can't have noisy neighbors impacting production latency.
[03:30] Maya: With Dedicated reserved nodes you get isolated GPU pools. We also offer tenancy guards — you can reserve nodes that are tenant-fenced so other customers won't be scheduled there; that reduces noisy neighbor risk. There's an isolation premium but it's predictable.
[03:52] Priya: About data at rest and keys — we need KMS integration and HSM options, plus audit trail for every call.
[03:58] Jonas: We support customer KMS, bring-your-own keys for Private and Dedicated through KMS connectors; HSM via enterprise add-on. Audit logs can be exported to your SIEM — we can show sample schema.

[05:30] Samir: What's the fallback story? If our reserved pool gets saturated during an extreme blast, can Redwood route to hosted spare capacity? We can't have complete outage.
[05:40] Maya: Yes — routing policy can do automatic fallback to compatible hosted variants in a different region or lower-cost quantized variants. You can set policies: strict (no fallback), recommended (failover to shared hosted with SLO warning), or hybrid.
[06:02] Samir: Any implications for data residency if we fallback to hosted?
[06:06] Priya: That's my concern. We have PII we can't send to multi-tenant hosted.
[06:10] Maya: Then we recommend Dedicated with no fallback to hosted for PII-sensitive routes; for less-sensitive routes you can enable fallbacks. Or we can do Dedicated + Private for the sensitive endpoints.

[08:00] Jonas: On burst modeling — prewarming helps but there's cost tradeoff. For example, keeping a hot pool sized for a 6k qps spike for several hours is expensive. We usually recommend probabilistic warm pools sized to 80th-90th percentile with auto-burst to additional reserved burst capacity. Also, returned suggestions: autoscale policy with burst credits.
[08:30] Lena: Can you explain burst credits?
[08:35] Jonas: Think of it like a banked credit where prewarm and short-term burst capacity can be consumed beyond baseline. It uses reserved capacity + ephemeral nodes to absorb very short spikes. Eviction risk exists for ephemeral nodes but reserved ones are sticky.

[10:10] Samir: How about GPU types? We're on A100s in prod today. What's the default for Dedicated?
[10:15] Maya: We support a range: A100, H100, and some Ampere/Inferentia variants depending on region. We can map your workload to recommended GPU SKU; Jonas can run a perf profile.
[10:28] Jonas: I'll ask for sample payloads and token distributions. We'll simulate with our micro-benchmark to recommend node size and number.

[12:05] Priya: On the security checklist — SSO (SAML/Okta), RBAC, organization-level audit, VPC peering, private networking, and per-tenant logging.
[12:15] Maya: All supported. For Dedicated we can do VPC peering, private endpoints, and SSO + RBAC. For Private/on-prem we can run a customer-managed control plane with your KMS.
[12:35] Priya: Do you have SOC2 Type II?
[12:38] Maya: Yes, SOC2 Type II. We can share the report under NDA.

[14:00] Lena: Pricing — are reserved nodes billed monthly? We want monthly commit with predictable unit pricing.
[14:08] Maya: Reserved capacity is monthly or annual commitments. We have reserved SKU pricing and a burst/ephemeral hourly rate for ephemeral nodes. I'll share the pricing sheet after the call.
[14:20] Samir: Any minimum commitment?
[14:22] Maya: Typically a small minimum depending on region — we'll include options in the pricing doc.

[16:45] Lena: On mixing Hosted and Dedicated — is it straightforward to use the same API? We want devs to have same interface across environments.
[16:53] Jonas: Yes — the API is consistent. You can pin route to a model in Dedicated or fallback to hosted. SDKs unify the calls. There are flags for region and tenancy.

[18:30] Samir: Network egress — we need to understand bandwidth across VPC peering for large payloads. Any recommendations?
[18:38] Maya: We'll share typical egress profiles. For heavy context workloads we recommend co-locating within same cloud region or using Private deployments to avoid cross-region egress.

[20:10] Jonas: A few technical notes: large session KV cache for long contexts requires more GPU RAM; quantized variants reduce RAM but may increase latency slightly. Also batching can save cost but increases p99 latency — you need to choose latency vs cost.
[20:35] Lena: Our SLO is 99th < 500ms for the interactive path. Is that realistic with 2-6k token contexts at burst?
[20:45] Jonas: It's tight. To hit p99 <500ms we recommend smaller quantized models for interactive, or a hybrid approach: use a smaller low-latency model as a quick responder and async a higher-quality model for long responses. Also ensure warm pool sized for the expected concurrency.

[23:00] Priya: For compliance we need retention choices — can Redwood not store logs or persist inputs?
[23:08] Maya: You can choose retention windows; for Dedicated we offer no-persists or ephemeral-only modes plus audit logs forwarded to your SIEM.

[25:30] Lena: We want to run a 48-hour spike simulation next week to see cost and latency profiles. Can Redwood run that on a staging account?
[25:40] Maya: Yes. Jonas will send a script and recommended load profile; we can coordinate a staging environment and reserve burst nodes for the window.

[27:50] Jonas: Actionable items I have: request sample payloads, token histogram, current p95/p99 latency per endpoint, and a short infra diagram. We'll produce a recommended node count and warm-pool sizing.
[28:10] Samir: I'll send sample logs and token distribution.

[30:00] Maya: A quick note on migration: switching routing from your in-house endpoints to Dedicated can be gradual; canary traffic to measure latency and cost, then ramp.
[30:15] Lena: Good.

[31:40] Priya: Also please include dataflow for KMS calls — we need to ensure keys never leave our VPC.
[31:46] Jonas: We'll include the KMS flow diagram. For Private/on-prem we can avoid key egress entirely.

[33:20] Lena: Competitors are pitching managed hosted with lower price per token. We care more about reliability and strict isolation for PII.
[33:32] Maya: Understood — that's where Dedicated and Private differ. Dedicated gives predictable nodes and VPC peering; Private hands off the control plane to you.

[35:00] Maya: Recap/next steps: we'll send pricing SKUs, SOC2 and security pack, perf profiling script, and propose a 48h burst simulation window. Jonas to own tech deep dive.
[35:15] Lena: Sounds good. We'll aim to get logs to you by Tue.

[37:00] Samir: One last question — do you support preemptible/spot nodes as a cheaper burst option?
[37:06] Jonas: Yes, ephemeral spot nodes can be used for non-sensitive workloads; they are best effort. We don't recommend them for PII or critical interactive paths.

[39:40] Maya: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with links and the pricing.
[39:46] Lena: Thanks, bye.
[39:48] Priya: Thank you.
[39:50] Samir: Bye.

End of transcript.
